title: NASA Takes Delivery of X-57, First All-Electric X-plane
description: The X-57 Maxwell, NASA’s first all-electric experimental aircraft, or X-plane – and the agency’s first crewed X-plane in two decades – was delivered by Empirical Systems Aerospace (ESAero) in the first of three configurations as an all-electric aircraft, known as Modification II, or Mod II.  X-57’s Mod II vehicle features the replacement of traditional combustion engines on a baseline Tecnam P2006T aircraft with electric cruise motors. The delivery is a major milestone for the project, allowing NASA engineers to begin putting the aircraft through ground tests, to be followed by taxi tests and eventually, flight tests.  A goal of the X-57 project is to help develop certification standards for emerging electric aircraft markets. NASA will share the aircraft’s electric-propulsion-focused design and airworthiness process with regulators and industry, which will advance certification approaches for aircraft using distributed electric propulsion.  The X-57 team is using a “design driver” as a technical challenge, to drive lessons learned and best practices. This design driver includes a 500% increase in high-speed cruise efficiency, zero in-flight carbon emissions, and flight that is much quieter for communities on the ground.
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: Huge milestone. The project consists of many stakeholders, but amongst the NASA team here,
everybody's very excited. It's a formal milestone and informally we're real excited about it.
X-57, it's a manned electric airplane and what we're doing is developing technologies
related to electric aircraft consisting of the motors, development of some safe battery systems,
and learning lessons along the way and pushing that out to other industry.
At one time it was a production Technum P-2006T, that's a twin engine trainer.
Now it's X-57 Mod 2 and it'll be an all-electric aircraft with about 850 pounds of batteries and
a single pilot and electric motors on the wing tip. So initially we started off doing wiring and
doing tests and turning it into an electric aircraft and then we started into actual functional
tests, ground tests, spinning propellers, things like that, doing a slow build-up approach on this
program. While this effort will be going on, Mod 3 with the smaller high-aspect ratio wing is
right now is leaving FRC and heading out to back to San Luis Obispo to ESAERO and that's where we'll
be performing fit checks on a tooling fuselage that we have there. We are trying to keep the
schedule compressed and so by having things run in a parallel effort then we don't have any delays.
Once we're done with Mod 2 testing we can move right into Mod 3.
